$comment: Herbs, teas, bush remedies and supplements (rule set supplement-catalogue, clinical-content/registry.json). The single source for web (artifacts/dashboard/src/lib/supplement-catalogue.ts) and iOS (SupplementCatalogue.swift, bundled folder "rules"). Validated by lint:shared-content. Items with interaction rules name a drug-classes term (drug-classes.ts / DrugClasses.swift), which holds their names. Stop times are clinician-facing only. text.herbalPreOpPatientText is the surgeon-approved patient paragraph (2026-09-25): change it only on his instruction; lint:patient-instructions pins it.

items.label: Garlic (supplement)
items.concern: Platelet inhibition; the strongest link to surgical bleeding, especially with anticoagulants
items.stopTime: at least 7 days; many advise 2 weeks
items.evidence: Evidence for cardiovascular claims is inconsistent. Normal amounts in food are not the concern.
items.source: Ang-Lee MK et al. JAMA 2001;286:208-16; Proc (Bayl Univ Med Cent) 2022

items.label: Ginkgo
items.concern: Platelet-activating factor inhibition; bleeding, especially with anticoagulants
items.stopTime: at least 36 hours; SPAQI advises 2 weeks
items.evidence: Evidence for cognitive claims is inconsistent.
items.source: Ang-Lee MK et al. JAMA 2001;286:208-16; OpenAnesthesia / SPAQI 2025

items.label: Ginger (supplement)
items.evidence: Normal amounts in food are not the concern; tablets, capsules, extracts and strong teas are.

items.label: Turmeric / curcumin
items.concern: Drug-induced liver injury (hepatocellular, typically 1–4 months after starting; linked to HLA-B*35:01); raises bleeding risk with anticoagulants
items.harms: Liver: US DILIN reported 10 cases (all since 2011), 5 hospitalised and 1 death from acute liver failure. Metal: some turmeric products have been adulterated with lead chromate.
items.evidence: Culinary turmeric is fine; the risk is high-dose, bioavailability-enhanced capsules (black pepper / piperine or nanoparticle forms). Benefit is weak beyond a small effect on osteoarthritis pain.
items.source: Halegoua-DeMarzio D et al. Am J Med 2023;136:200-206 (DILIN); J Clin Anesth 2024 review

items.label: Ashwagandha
items.concern: Drug-induced liver injury, typically cholestatic with severe jaundice and itch, resolving over 1–5 months, sometimes fatal
items.harms: Liver: LiverTox lists it as a likely cause of clinically apparent liver injury. Denmark banned ashwagandha supplements in 2023 (thyroid and sex-hormone effects). Avoid in liver disease, pregnancy and thyroid disease.
items.evidence: Small trials suggest reduced perceived stress.
items.source: NIDDK LiverTox: Ashwagandha (Dec 2024); Björnsson HK et al. Liver Int 2020;40:825-9

items.label: Ginseng
items.concern: Hypoglycaemia, especially in fasting patients (pre-op fast or religious fast); possible platelet effects; reduced INR reported with warfarin
items.stopTime: at least 7 days; SPAQI advises 2 weeks
items.evidence: Evidence for energy and cognitive claims is inconsistent.
items.source: Ang-Lee MK et al. JAMA 2001;286:208-16; OpenAnesthesia / SPAQI 2025

items.label: St John's wort
items.concern: CYP3A4 induction: lowers levels of warfarin, ciclosporin, tacrolimus, DOACs, hormonal contraceptives and many anaesthetic drugs; serotonin syndrome with serotonergic drugs
items.source: Ang-Lee MK et al. JAMA 2001;286:208-16; BNF interactions (St John's wort)

items.label: Valerian
items.concern: Potentiates anaesthetic sedation; stopping suddenly can cause a benzodiazepine-like withdrawal
items.stopTime: taper over 1–2 weeks (do not stop suddenly)

items.label: Echinacea
items.concern: Immune effects; avoid if immunosuppression is planned

items.label: Ephedra (ma huang)
items.concern: Hypertension and arrhythmia (sympathomimetic); interacts with MAOIs and anaesthesia
items.stopTime: at least 24 hours; ideally avoid entirely
items.harms: Whole-herb ephedra weight-loss supplements caused cardiovascular deaths and were banned by the US FDA in 2004.

items.label: Ayurvedic preparation (rasa shastra / metal-based)
items.harms: Metal: 20.7% of Ayurvedic medicines bought online (US- and Indian-made) contained lead, mercury or arsenic; metal-based rasa shastra products were more than twice as likely to contain metals; a 2015 review attributed 19% of published lead-poisoning cases to Ayurvedic medicines.
items.source: Saper RB et al. JAMA 2008;300:915-23; Public Health Ontario fact sheet (2019)

items.label: Chinese herbal slimming product (aristolochic acid risk)
items.names: aristolochia|aristolochic acid|aristolochia fangchi|guang fang ji|chinese herbal slimming|chinese slimming|slimming pills|herbal weight-loss
items.concern: Aristolochic acid nephropathy (rapidly progressive kidney failure) and upper-tract urothelial carcinoma
items.harms: Renal and cancer: in the Belgian slimming-pill cluster (Stephania tetrandra substituted with Aristolochia fangchi) more than 100 women developed rapidly progressive kidney failure; 46% of 39 who later had prophylactic ureteronephrectomy had urothelial cancer.
items.source: Nortier JL et al. N Engl J Med 2000;342:1686-92; Debelle FD et al. Kidney Int 2008

items.label: Detox tea / colon cleanse / laxative cleanse
items.names: detox tea|detox teas|colon cleanse|colon cleansing|cleanse tea|laxative tea|slimming tea|skinny tea|body cleanse
items.evidence: No reliable evidence of benefit beyond placebo.

items.label: IV vitamin drip (outside clinical care)
items.names: iv vitamin drip|vitamin drip|iv vitamin infusion|iv drip therapy|myers cocktail|iv glutathione
items.evidence: Little outcome evidence for healthy people outside specific medical indications.

items.label: Spermidine / "autophagy booster"
items.concern: No benefit shown in humans (SmartAge RCT)
items.evidence: The 12-month placebo-controlled SmartAge trial (100 older adults) found no improvement in memory or biomarkers. Recording it is enough.
items.source: Schwarz C et al. JAMA Netw Open 2022;5:e2213875 (SmartAge)

items.label: Bush tea / herbal remedy (unspecified)
items.names: bush tea|bush medicine|bush remedy|herbal tea|herbal remedy|herbal mixture|herbal medicine
items.concern: Plant not identified: interactions and perioperative risk unknown
items.stopTime: identify the plant; stop non-essential herbal products 1–2 weeks before elective surgery (ASA / SPAQI) — clinician to confirm
items.source: ASA / SPAQI (OpenAnesthesia 2025); J Clin Anesth 2024 review

text.patientQuestion: Do you take any herbs, bush teas, bush medicines, vitamins or supplements? Please include teas and remedies from the garden or market.
text.disclosureRationale: 50–70% of surgical patients do not disclose herbal use (J Clin Anesth 2024 review). Ask explicitly, including local bush teas, which patients often do not count as medicine.
text.herbalPreOpPatientText: Herbal remedies, bush teas and supplements: please stop them 2 weeks before your operation or procedure. This includes garlic tablets, ginkgo, ginseng, ginger supplements, turmeric (curcumin), St John's wort, kava, echinacea, ashwagandha, ephedra (ma huang) and bush teas or herbal mixtures (tablets, capsules, extracts or strong teas — normal amounts in food are fine). Why: some of these increase bleeding, change how the anaesthetic or sedation works, raise blood pressure or blood sugar problems, or stop your other medicines working properly. When: this applies to planned operations and to procedures with sedation or an anaesthetic, including gastroscopy, colonoscopy and ERCP. If your operation is less than 2 weeks away, stop them now and tell the team what you take. If you take valerian every night, do not stop it suddenly — call the clinic. This does not apply to medicines prescribed by a doctor: do not stop any prescribed medicine unless the clinic tells you to. Please bring all your herbs, teas and supplements (or their labels) to your appointment.

prompts.title: Herbs, teas, bush remedies & supplements not asked
prompts.detail: 50–70% of surgical patients do not disclose herbal use (J Clin Anesth 2024 review). Ask explicitly, including local bush teas, and record the answer (none, or what is taken).

prompts.title: Ashwagandha: avoid in liver disease, pregnancy and thyroid disease (LiverTox; Danish ban 2023)
prompts.detail: Ashwagandha is recorded and the record shows liver disease, pregnancy or thyroid disease. Decision support only — the clinician decides.

prompts.title: Raised LFTs / hepatitis — ask about herbal products
prompts.detail: If unexplained, ask about turmeric / curcumin (especially capsules with black pepper / piperine), ashwagandha and other herbal products: herbal liver injury is often not volunteered (DILIN; LiverTox).

prompts.title: Anaemia, abdominal pain, neuropathy or raised lead — ask about Ayurvedic products
prompts.detail: If unexplained, ask about Ayurvedic (rasa shastra) preparations and turmeric products (some adulterated with lead chromate); consider a blood lead level (Saper JAMA 2008).

prompts.title: Renal failure or upper-tract urothelial cancer — ask about Chinese herbal products
prompts.detail: Ask about Chinese herbal products, slimming pills and Chinese herbal weight-loss products (aristolochic acid nephropathy and urothelial carcinoma: Nortier NEJM 2000; Debelle Kidney Int 2008).

prompts.title: Low potassium or sodium, dehydration or chronic constipation — ask about detox teas and cleanses
prompts.detail: If unexplained, ask about detox teas, colon cleanses and laxative "cleanse" products (dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, laxative dependence).

prompts.title: Fever or skin / line-site infection — ask about IV drips
prompts.detail: Ask about recent IV vitamin drips given outside clinical care (infection and fluid risks).

prompts.title: Decision support only
prompts.detail: The clinician decides whether anything is stopped; nothing is stopped automatically.
